title: Fast Cliffords When Your Quantum Memory Is Full
authors: Marten Folkertsma, Ian Mertz, Sergii Strelchuk, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian
abstract: Additional qubits can reduce the depth of a quantum circuit by providing workspace for parallel computation, but standard constructions assume that this workspace is initialized in a known state. In this work we study catalytic implementations, i.e. asking whether dirty qubits can instead be used provided that their joint state including any entanglement with other registers is restored exactly at the end of the computation. We show that every $n$-qubit Clifford circuit has a catalytic implementation of depth $O(\log n)$ using $O(n^2/\log^2 n)$ catalytic qubits and no clean qubits, matching the asymptotic depth achievable when clean workspace is available. We extend this approach to diagonal elements of any fixed level $C_k$ of the Clifford hierarchy, which admit catalytic implementations of depth $O(\log(n+1))$ with $O(n^k/\log(n))$ gates and $O(n^k/\log^2(n))$ catalytic qubits, as well as to semi-Clifford Gates.
summary: This paper demonstrates that the computational depth of Clifford circuits can be maintained at an optimal $O(\log n)$ scaling even when using only 'catalytic' qubits instead of clean ancillas. By employing algebraic cancellation techniques, the authors show that this catalytic memory approach is sufficient for implementing complex quantum operations efficiently. This advances the understanding of resource trade-offs in quantum circuit design.
main_problem: The paper investigates replacing the need for clean (known initial state) ancillary qubits in quantum circuits with 'catalytic' qubits, which must have their joint state restored at the end of the computation.
main_result: They show that every $n$-qubit Clifford circuit can be implemented catalytically with depth $O(\log n)$ using $O(n^2 / \log^2 n)$ catalytic qubits, matching the best achievable depth.
method: The authors use algebraic cancellation techniques, building on the Clifford normal form, to eliminate the dependence on the unknown initial state of the catalytic qubits.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum circuits, specifically Clifford circuits and diagonal unitaries belonging to the Clifford hierarchy ($C_k$). The model distinguishes between clean ancillas (starting in $|0angle$) and catalytic ancillas (starting in an arbitrary state $|	auangle$).
key_observables: Depth of the circuit (e.g., $O(\log n)$), required number of catalytic qubits (e.g., $O(n^2 / \log^2 n)$), and the absence of clean qubits.
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), the level of the Clifford hierarchy ($k$), and the depth scaling factor ($\log n$).
main_assumptions: The results are established for Clifford and semi-Clifford circuits; the conjecture for general quantum circuits remains open.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the catalytic implementation for general Clifford circuits, then extending the technique to diagonal elements of the Clifford hierarchy, and finally addressing semi-Clifford gates, always aiming to maintain logarithmic depth scaling.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool for resource-constrained quantum computation, showing how to achieve optimal depth scaling without requiring perfect, clean quantum memory.
